micro_skills.micro_skill: Verify one-to-one and find the inverse algebraically
definitions: f is one-to-one if x1 ≠ x2 in the domain implies f(x1) ≠ f(x2), equivalently f(x1)=f(x2) ⇒ x1=x2. Geometrically: every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.
Any function that is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval is automatically one-to-one there.
If f is one-to-one, its inverse f^-1 is defined by y = f^-1(x) ⇔ x = f(y).
f is self-inverse if f^-1 = f (e.g. f(x)=1/x).
formulas: domain of f^-1 = range of f; range of f^-1 = domain of f
f^-1(f(x)) = x for all x in domain of f
f(f^-1(x)) = x for all x in domain of f^-1
graph of f^-1 = reflection of graph of f in the line y=x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Show that a given linear or simple polynomial/rational f is one-to-one by checking f'(x) has constant sign, then solve x=f(y) for y to find f^-1(x).
question_archetypes.example: Show f(x) = 2x - 1 is one-to-one and find f^-1.
question_archetypes.answer: f'(x)=2>0 everywhere so f is increasing, hence one-to-one; f^-1(x) = (x+1)/2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is a simple algebraic expression and the question says 'show it has an inverse' or 'is one-to-one' — the fastest route is a derivative sign check, not the x1=x2 definition.
method_plan: Compute f'(x) and determine its sign on the whole domain
Conclude monotonic ⇒ one-to-one
Set y = f^-1(x), write x = f(y), solve algebraically for y in terms of x
State f^-1(x)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivative and sign argument for monotonicity
A1: correct algebraic solve for y
A1: f^-1 stated in function notation, matching variable

common_errors.description: Solving for x instead of y (mixing up which variable is the input to f^-1)
Never explicitly stating the one-to-one conclusion before writing the inverse

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Show f is one-to-one using the algebraic definition f(x1)=f(x2) ⇒ x1=x2 (useful when f' is awkward, e.g. involves a square root), then find f^-1 and its domain.
question_archetypes.example: Show g(x) = sqrt(2x+1) is invertible and find g^-1.
question_archetypes.answer: g is increasing on its domain x ≥ -1/2 (one-to-one); g^-1(x) = (x^2-1)/2 for x ≥ 0.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function involves a radical or awkward algebraic form where differentiating to check sign is more work than directly assuming g(x1)=g(x2) and manipulating the equation until x1=x2 falls out.
method_plan: Assume g(x1) = g(x2)
Manipulate algebraically (e.g. square both sides) to derive x1 = x2
Conclude one-to-one
Solve x = g(y) for y, tracking any sign/domain restriction introduced (e.g. y ≥ 0)
State g^-1 together with its domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct one-to-one argument from the algebraic definition
M1: correct solve for the inverse
A1: correct stated domain of g^-1 (matching the range of g)

common_errors.description: Omitting the domain restriction on f^-1 entirely
Sign error when squaring/un-squaring a radical equation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given f not one-to-one on its natural domain, restrict the domain to a monotone piece, then find the inverse of the restriction, stating domain/range.
question_archetypes.example: Let f(x) = x^2 for x ≥ 0. Find f^-1 and state its domain and range.
question_archetypes.answer: f^-1(x) = sqrt(x), domain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The stated domain of f is explicitly restricted (e.g. 'x ≥ 0') rather than all reals — signal that f fails the horizontal line test on its natural domain and the restriction is what makes inversion possible.
method_plan: Confirm f is one-to-one on the restricted domain given
Solve x = f(y) for y on that restricted piece, choosing the correct branch/sign
State f^-1 with domain = range of the restricted f and range = the restricted domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct branch chosen when solving (e.g. positive square root)
A1: correct f^-1 formula
A1: domain and range of f^-1 stated correctly

common_errors.description: Not restricting the domain first and trying to invert x^2 directly (fails the one-to-one requirement)
Choosing the wrong branch of the square/nth-root when solving for y

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the boxed inverse-function properties (f^-1(f(x))=x, reflection in y=x, domain/range swap) to answer a conceptual or graph-based question without fully solving for f^-1.
question_archetypes.example: If f(3) = 7 and f is one-to-one, state f^-1(7) and describe how the graph of f^-1 relates to the graph of f.
question_archetypes.answer: f^-1(7) = 3; the graph of f^-1 is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question gives a specific function value or asks about the graph relationship rather than asking to 'find f^-1(x)' as a formula — a cue to use the definitional properties directly instead of algebra.
method_plan: Apply y = f^-1(x) ⇔ x = f(y) directly to the given data point
State the reflection-in-y=x graph property if asked about the graph
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct value via the defining property (no need to find f^-1 explicitly)
A1: correct statement of the graph reflection property if requested

common_errors.description: Confusing f^-1(x) with 1/f(x) when reading off the value
Failing to justify the point swap (x,y)→(y,x) reasoning

micro_skills.micro_skill: Differentiate an inverse function using the inverse-derivative formula
definitions: Obtained by differentiating f(f^-1(x)) = x with the Chain Rule.

theorems.name: Derivative of an inverse function
theorems.statement: If f is differentiable and monotonic on (a,b) with f'(x) ≠ 0, then d/dx[f^-1(x)] = 1 / f'(f^-1(x)).
conditions: f monotonic (strictly increasing or decreasing) on (a,b)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given f(a) = b for a specific numeric a, find (f^-1)'(b) using the formula without finding f^-1 explicitly (typically because f^-1 has no elementary closed form).
question_archetypes.example: Let f(x) = x^3 + x. Since f(2) = 10, find (f^-1)'(10).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives a function value f(a)=b and asks for the derivative of the inverse at b — an explicit closed form for f^-1 is not requested or not obtainable, signaling 'use the formula, not algebra.'
method_plan: Verify f is monotonic (f'(x) ≠ 0 everywhere) so the inverse exists and is differentiable
Identify f^-1(b) = a using the given data point
Compute f'(a)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies f^-1(b) = a from the given value (not solving for f^-1 directly)
M1: correct computation of f'(a)
A1: correct final reciprocal

common_errors.description: Trying to find f^-1(x) explicitly by inverting a cubic instead of using the formula
Plugging b (not a = f^-1(b)) into f'(x) — the classic 'wrong argument' error

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given an explicitly invertible f, find f^-1 directly, differentiate it, and separately verify the same result using the inverse-derivative formula.
question_archetypes.example: If f(x) = x^2 for x ≥ 0, find f^-1 and verify (f^-1)'(4) two ways.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The prompt explicitly says 'verify two ways' or 'confirm using the formula' — requires both direct differentiation of f^-1 and the reciprocal-derivative formula.
method_plan: Find f^-1(x) explicitly and differentiate directly
Evaluate at the given point
Separately compute f^-1 of the point and f' at that value, then take the reciprocal
Confirm both answers match
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct explicit f^-1 and its derivative
A1: correct value from direct differentiation
M1: correct application of the formula as a check
A1: both methods reconciled

common_errors.description: Arithmetic slip evaluating the derivative at the specific point
Not showing the reconciliation between the two methods when asked to verify

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate y = f^-1(x) symbolically to derive a general formula (e.g. rediscovering d/dx sqrt(x) or an inverse-trig derivative from first principles using this theorem).
question_archetypes.example: Use the inverse-function derivative formula to find d/dx[sin^-1(x)] starting from f(y) = sin y on [-π/2, π/2].
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question says 'derive' or 'use the inverse function theorem to find the derivative of...' pointing at a known inverse (inverse trig, nth root) rather than asking to just quote the memorized formula.
method_plan: Let y = f^-1(x) so x = f(y)
Apply the formula dy/dx = 1/f'(y)
Express f'(y) in terms of x using x = f(y) and (if needed) a Pythagorean/algebraic identity
State the final derivative purely in terms of x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct setup x = f(y), dy/dx = 1/f'(y)
M1: correct substitution back to a function of x using an identity
A1: fully simplified final formula

common_errors.description: Leaving the answer in terms of y instead of converting back to x
Sign error when taking the square root to convert cos y (or similar) into a function of x

micro_skills.micro_skill: Simplify expressions using the laws of exponents and logarithms
definitions: For a>0: a^0=1; a^n = a·a···a (n factors); a^-n = 1/a^n; a^(m/n) = nth-root(a^m).
For a>0, a≠1: y = log_a x ⇔ x = a^y. Domain of log_a is (0,∞); range is ℝ.
Cancellation identities: log_a(a^x) = x, a^(log_a x) = x.
formulas: log_a 1 = 0, log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y, log_a(1/x) = -log_a x
log_a(x/y) = log_a x - log_a y, log_a(x^y) = y·log_a x
change of base: log_a x = log_b x / log_b a

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Combine a sum/difference of logarithms (same base) into a single log using the product/quotient rules and evaluate.
question_archetypes.example: Simplify log_2(10) + log_2(12) - log_2(15).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Several log terms with the same base are added and subtracted — combine into one log of a product/quotient before evaluating, rather than trying to evaluate each log separately.
method_plan: Combine all + terms into a single log of a product
Combine all - terms by dividing
Simplify the resulting argument numerically
Evaluate the single logarithm
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct use of product rule to combine additive terms
M1: correct use of quotient rule to combine subtractive terms
A1: correct final numeric evaluation

common_errors.description: Writing log(x+y) = log x + log y (invalid — only products split this way)
Arithmetic slip combining the fraction inside the log before evaluating

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Simplify an expression like a^(log_b c) using change of base to rewrite the exponent in base a, then simplify the power.
question_archetypes.example: Simplify 3^(log_9 4).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An exponential expression has a logarithm with a different base than the exponential base itself — the mismatch is the cue to change base so exponent and base line up.
method_plan: Rewrite log_9 4 in base 3 using change-of-base: log_9 4 = log_3 4 / log_3 9
Simplify log_3 9 = 2
Use cancellation 3^(log_3 4) = 4, then take the square root
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct change of base applied
M1: correct use of cancellation identity a^(log_a x) = x
A1: correct final numeric answer

common_errors.description: Trying to evaluate log_9 4 as a decimal instead of using the cancellation identity
Mishandling the fractional exponent when splitting the power

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a purely numeric expression involving exponents/logs using the laws (no unknown x), e.g. simplifying a product of powers with different bases sharing a common base.
question_archetypes.answer: 2 (rewrite all terms as powers of 2: 2^5 · 2^-4 / 2^1 = 2^0... recompute carefully: 2^5·2^-4=2^1, divided by 2^1 = 2^0=1). [Answer depends on exact numbers used in the drill instance.]
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: All bases in the expression are powers of a common base (e.g. 2, 4, 8 are all powers of 2) — rewrite everything with that common base before combining exponents.
method_plan: Rewrite every term as a power of the common base
Combine exponents using the exponent laws
Simplify to a single power
Evaluate numerically if required
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrites all terms with a common base
M1: correct exponent arithmetic combining terms
A1: correct final simplified value

common_errors.description: Exponent arithmetic slip when combining terms with a common base
Forgetting to convert every term to the common base before combining

micro_skills.micro_skill: Solve equations with the unknown in an exponent or inside a logarithm
definitions: Solving an exponential equation typically requires taking ln (or log) of both sides to bring the unknown out of the exponent.
Solving a logarithmic equation requires exponentiating, and always checking candidate solutions lie in the domain x>0 of every log involved.
formulas: a^x = b ⇔ x = ln b / ln a (any base works, ln is conventional)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve an equation with different bases raised to expressions involving x by taking ln of both sides and isolating x.
question_archetypes.example: Solve 3^(x-1) = 2^x for x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The unknown x appears only in exponents with two different bases that are not simple powers of each other — signals 'take ln of both sides' rather than trying to equalize bases.
method_plan: Take ln of both sides
Use ln(a^k) = k·ln a to bring exponents down as multipliers
Collect all x terms on one side
Factor out x and divide to solve; give exact and decimal forms if requested
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly applies ln to both sides and the power rule
M1: correctly collects x terms and factors
A1: correct exact form
A1: correct decimal approximation

common_errors.description: Sign error collecting x terms (e.g. x ln3 - x ln2 vs x ln2 - x ln3)
Giving only a decimal approximation when an exact expression was requested

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve a logarithmic equation (possibly quadratic in the log or with logs of linear expressions) and reject any solution outside the domain of the original logs.
question_archetypes.example: Solve log_2(x) + log_2(x-2) = 3.
question_archetypes.answer: x = 4 (the other algebraic root x = -2 is rejected since log_2(-2) is undefined).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The equation contains log of an expression in x (not just log of x alone), so solving algebraically can generate extraneous roots that must be checked against x>0 for every log argument.
method_plan: Combine logs into a single log using the product/quotient rules
Exponentiate both sides to clear the log
Solve the resulting polynomial/algebraic equation for x
Check every candidate root against the domain of each original log term and reject invalid ones
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct combination of logs
M1: correct exponentiation and resulting equation solved
A1: correct identification and rejection of the extraneous root
A1: correct final valid solution stated

common_errors.description: Not checking the domain and reporting an extraneous root as valid
Error solving the resulting quadratic/polynomial equation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve an exponential equation where both sides can be rewritten as powers of the same base without needing logarithms.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both numeric bases are powers of a small common integer (2, 3, e, etc.) — recognizing this avoids needing logarithms at all; a faster, cleaner method than taking ln.
method_plan: Rewrite each base as a power of a common integer
Use (a^m)^n = a^(mn) to write both sides as that common base to a single exponent
Equate the exponents (valid since a^u=a^v ⇒ u=v for a>0,a≠1)
Solve the resulting linear/polynomial equation for x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrites both sides with a common base
M1: correctly equates exponents
A1: correct final solution

common_errors.description: Taking logarithms of both sides when a common-base shortcut was available (not wrong, but inefficient and more error-prone)
Distributing the exponent incorrectly, e.g. 2(x+1) mis-expanded

micro_skills.subtopic: Derivatives of ln, exp, and general exponential/log functions
micro_skills.micro_skill: Differentiate composite functions built from ln, e^x, and general a^x / log_a x
definitions: For x>0, ln x is defined as the signed area under y=1/t between t=1 and t=x.
exp x is defined as the inverse of ln x; e = exp(1) ≈ 2.718281828...; exp x = e^x for all real x.
General exponential: a^x = e^(x ln a) for a>0.
d/dx ln|x| = 1/x for all x≠0, so ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C.

theorems.name: General Power Rule
theorems.statement: d/dx x^a = a·x^(a-1) for x>0 and any real a, derived from x^a = e^(a ln x).

formulas: d/dx e^x = e^x, ∫e^x dx = e^x + C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate y = e^(g(x)) for a polynomial or simple inner function g(x) using the Chain Rule.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = e^(x^2 - 3x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The base is e with a non-trivial exponent (not just x) — the Chain Rule factor g'(x) must multiply the unchanged e^(g(x)).
method_plan: Identify the inner function g(x) in the exponent
Differentiate g(x)
Write y' = g'(x)·e^(g(x))
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct inner derivative g'(x)
A1: correctly multiplied by the unchanged e^(g(x))

common_errors.description: Forgetting the chain-rule factor g'(x) entirely (treating e^(g(x)) as if it differentiates to itself)
Error differentiating the polynomial exponent g(x)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate y = ln(g(x)) for a composite inner function using d/dx ln(g(x)) = g'(x)/g(x).
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = ln(sec x + tan x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A logarithm wraps a non-trivial inner expression — apply the chain rule as (inner derivative)/(inner function), then simplify algebraically/trigonometrically.
method_plan: Identify the inner function g(x) inside ln(·)
Differentiate g(x)
Write y' = g'(x)/g(x)
Simplify algebraically (factor, cancel) to the cleanest form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct inner derivative
M1: correct chain-rule quotient set up
A1: fully simplified final answer

common_errors.description: Forgetting the chain rule and writing y' = 1/g(x) with no g'(x) factor
Missing an algebraic/trig simplification that the problem expects (e.g. not factoring sec x out)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate a general exponential a^(g(x)) or logarithm log_a(g(x)) with base a≠e, using the ln-a factor.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = 5^(x^2) and y = log_3(2x+1).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The base of the exponential/log is a specific number other than e — the extra factor ln a (or division by ln a) is required, unlike the e^x / ln x case.
method_plan: Recall d/dx a^u = a^u·ln a·u' and d/dx log_a u = u'/(u·ln a)
Identify u(x) and compute u'(x)
Substitute into the appropriate formula
Simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct formula selected with the ln a factor included
M1: correct chain-rule derivative of the inner function
A1: correctly simplified final answer for both parts

common_errors.description: Omitting the ln a factor and treating a^x like e^x
Forgetting the chain-rule inner derivative u'(x)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate ln of an expression containing a square root or sum with a radical, requiring simplification after the chain rule (often collapsing to a surprisingly simple result).
question_archetypes.example: Find d/dx ln(x + sqrt(x^2+1)).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The argument of ln contains x plus a square-root term of a similar form (a classic 'this simplifies dramatically' setup related to inverse hyperbolic functions) — expect heavy algebraic cancellation after differentiating.
method_plan: Differentiate the inner expression x + sqrt(x^2+1), using the chain rule on the square root
Divide by the original inner expression (chain rule for ln)
Factor sqrt(x^2+1) from numerator and denominator to cancel the (x + sqrt(x^2+1)) factor
State the simplified final answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivative of the inner radical expression
M1: correct chain-rule quotient formed
A1: fully simplified answer after cancellation

common_errors.description: Failing to spot the common factor that cancels, leaving an unsimplified (and ungraded-as-complete) answer
Chain rule error differentiating sqrt(x^2+1) (missing the x/sqrt(x^2+1) factor)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Differentiate products/quotients of many factors or variable-exponent expressions via logarithmic differentiation
definitions: For y=[f(x)]^g(x) or for products/quotients of many factors, take ln of both sides first, then differentiate implicitly; this converts products/quotients to sums/differences and handles variable exponents.
formulas: ln|y| = sum of ln|factors|  ⇒  y'/y = sum of (factor')/(factor)  ⇒  y' = y · (sum of (factor')/(factor))

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate a product/quotient of three or more linear (or simple) factors using logarithmic differentiation instead of repeated product/quotient rule.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = [(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)]/(x+4) using logarithmic differentiation.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Three or more factors are multiplied/divided together — direct product/quotient rule would be tedious; taking ln first converts everything to a sum, which is much faster to differentiate.
method_plan: Take ln|y| of both sides and expand using log laws into a sum/difference of ln|factor| terms
Differentiate implicitly: d/dx ln|y| = y'/y
Differentiate each ln|factor| term to get factor'/factor
Solve for y' by multiplying both sides by y (substitute the original expression for y)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct expansion of ln|y| into sum of logs
M1: correct implicit differentiation term by term
A1: correctly solved for y' with y substituted back in

common_errors.description: Forgetting to multiply back by y at the end (leaving the answer as y'/y)
Sign error on the subtracted (denominator) term

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate y = x^x or a similar 'variable base, variable exponent' expression by writing y=e^(x ln x) or by taking ln of both sides.
question_archetypes.example: Find the critical point of y = x^x for x>0.
question_archetypes.answer: Critical point at x = 1/e (since y' = x^x(1+ln x) = 0 ⇒ ln x = -1).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both the base and the exponent contain the variable x (x^x, or more generally f(x)^g(x)) — neither the Power Rule nor the exponential rule alone applies; this is the signature case for logarithmic differentiation.
method_plan: Take ln of both sides: ln y = x ln x
Differentiate implicitly using the product rule on the right: y'/y = ln x + 1
Solve for y' = y(ln x + 1) = x^x(1+ln x)
If asked for a critical point, set y'=0 and solve (noting y=x^x>0 never vanishes, so 1+ln x=0)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct implicit ln differentiation using product rule
A1: correct final derivative with y substituted back
M1: correctly sets the bracket factor to zero
A1: correct critical point value

common_errors.description: Trying to use the ordinary Power Rule (nx^(n-1)) on x^x, which does not apply since the exponent is also variable
Forgetting the product rule when differentiating x ln x on the right-hand side

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate y=[f(x)]^(g(x)) for general (non-x) f and g using logarithmic differentiation.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = (sin x)^(cos x).
question_archetypes.answer: y' = (sin x)^(cos x) · [-sin x·ln(sin x) + cos x·cot x].
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both the base f(x) and exponent g(x) are non-constant functions of x (not just x itself) — a strictly more general version of the x^x pattern, still requiring logarithmic differentiation.
method_plan: Take ln of both sides: ln y = g(x)·ln f(x)
Differentiate the right side with the product rule: (ln y)' = g'(x)ln f(x) + g(x)·f'(x)/f(x)
Multiply both sides by y = [f(x)]^(g(x)) to isolate y'
Substitute back f, g explicitly and simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct ln y = g ln f setup
M1: correct product-rule differentiation of the right side
A1: correctly multiplied back by y with f,g substituted
A1: reasonable simplification shown

common_errors.description: Missing the product rule and only differentiating one of g(x)ln f(x)'s two factors
Chain rule slip differentiating ln f(x) itself, i.e. dropping the f'(x)/f(x) factor

micro_skills.micro_skill: Correctly identify whether an expression is a power function, an exponential function, or requires logarithmic differentiation
definitions: x^a (variable base, constant exponent) is a power function — use the Power/General Power Rule.
a^x (constant base, variable exponent) is an exponential function — use d/dx a^x = a^x ln a.
x^x, f(x)^g(x), or products/quotients of many variable factors require logarithmic differentiation — neither of the above rules alone applies.
formulas: x^a → a·x^(a-1);  a^x → a^x·ln a;  [f(x)]^(g(x)) → logarithmic differentiation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given several superficially similar expressions (x^5, 5^x, x^x), state which differentiation rule applies to each before differentiating.
question_archetypes.example: For y1=x^7, y2=7^x, y3=x^7 + 7^x, y4=x^x, state which rule(s) apply and differentiate each.
question_archetypes.answer: y1'=7x^6 (Power Rule); y2'=7^x ln7 (exponential rule); y3'=7x^6+7^x ln7 (sum of both); y4'=x^x(1+ln x) (logarithmic differentiation).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A list or mixed expression contains both x^(constant) and (constant)^x forms side by side — the deliberate visual similarity is the trap; check which piece (base or exponent) is the variable.
method_plan: For each term, identify whether the variable is in the base, the exponent, or both
Apply Power Rule if variable is only in the base
Apply a^x·ln a rule if variable is only in the exponent
Apply logarithmic differentiation if variable is in both
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct rule identified for each term
A1: correct derivative for the power-function term(s)
A1: correct derivative for the exponential term(s)
A1: correct derivative for any mixed term via log differentiation

common_errors.description: Applying the Power Rule to a^x (treating x as the base) or the exponential rule to x^a (treating a as the base)
Missing the ln a factor on an exponential term

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate a sum/difference containing a mix of power, exponential, and log terms in one expression.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = 3x^4 - 2^x + ln(5x) - x^(1/2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Multiple distinct term types are added together (polynomial, exponential base a≠e, ln, fractional power) — each term must be routed to its own correct rule and then summed via linearity.
method_plan: Split the sum into individual terms
Differentiate each term with its appropriate rule (power, exponential-base-a, ln chain rule)
Add the results (linearity of differentiation)
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct power-rule term(s)
A1: correct exponential term with ln a factor
A1: correct ln-chain-rule term
A1: all terms correctly summed with signs preserved

common_errors.description: Using the wrong rule on one term while correctly handling the others
Sign error carried through from the original expression

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Apply the correct rule (logarithmic differentiation) to find and classify a critical point of a genuinely mixed-variable expression like x^x, distinguishing it from a similar-looking power or exponential function.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why d/dx(x^x) ≠ x·x^(x-1) and ≠ x^x·ln x, then find the correct derivative and its critical point.
question_archetypes.answer: Both proposed shortcuts are wrong because x^x is neither a pure power nor a pure exponential; correct derivative is x^x(1+ln x), critical point x=1/e.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly asks to explain a common misconception about which rule applies to x^x — a conceptual/diagnostic archetype rather than a pure computation.
method_plan: State why the Power Rule fails (exponent is not constant)
State why the pure exponential rule fails (base is not constant)
Apply logarithmic differentiation correctly
Solve for the critical point
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct explanation of why Power Rule doesn't apply
A1: correct explanation of why exponential rule doesn't apply
M1: correct logarithmic-differentiation derivative
A1: correct critical point

common_errors.description: Applying either the Power Rule or exponential rule to x^x despite both being invalid here
Giving the correct final derivative without any justification when the question asks for explanation

micro_skills.subtopic: Basic Integrals Involving ln and exp
micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate basic integrals that produce ln or exponential antiderivatives
definitions: ∫e^x dx = e^x + C.
∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C for x≠0.
More generally, ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C whenever the numerator is (a constant multiple of) the derivative of the denominator.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate e^(kx+b) for constants k,b, remembering to divide by the inner-derivative constant k.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate ∫e^(3x-1) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The exponent is a linear function of x (not just x) — reverse chain rule requires dividing by the coefficient of x.
method_plan: Identify the inner linear function and its derivative (a constant k)
Write the antiderivative as (1/k)e^(inner)
Add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the 1/k scaling factor
A1: correct final antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting to divide by k (treating ∫e^(kx)dx as if it were e^(kx))
Omitting +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate 1/(ax+b) using the ln|·| antiderivative, dividing by the coefficient a.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate ∫ dx/(2x+5).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a constant over a linear expression — recognize the ln|linear| antiderivative pattern with the 1/(coefficient of x) scaling.
method_plan: Recognize the form 1/(linear) matches d/dx ln|linear| up to a constant
Divide by the coefficient of x inside
Write the antiderivative with the absolute value and +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct recognition of the ln form
A1: correct scaling constant and final answer with |·| and +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the 1/(coefficient) scaling factor
Omitting the absolute value bars or +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize an integrand of the form f'(x)/f(x) (numerator is exactly, or a constant multiple of, the derivative of the denominator) and integrate directly to ln|f(x)|+C.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate ∫ (2x-3)/(x^2-3x+7) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator (or a constant multiple of it) — a strong visual cue that no substitution algebra is needed beyond recognizing this pattern.
method_plan: Differentiate the denominator mentally and compare to the numerator
If they match (up to a constant multiple), write the antiderivative as (constant)·ln|denominator|
Adjust for any constant multiple mismatch
Add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies numerator as (a multiple of) the derivative of the denominator
A1: correct antiderivative with any necessary constant adjustment and +C

common_errors.description: Missing the f'/f pattern entirely and attempting a much harder technique (e.g. partial fractions) unnecessarily
Constant-multiple mismatch not corrected for (e.g. numerator is 2× the true derivative but this isn't accounted for)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Set up and solve the exponential growth/decay model dy/dt = ky from data
definitions: If dy/dt = ky, the general solution is y = Ce^(kt).
The initial-value problem y' = ky, y(0)=y0 has the unique solution y(t) = y0·e^(kt).
k>0 gives exponential growth; k<0 gives exponential decay.

theorems.name: ln x ≤ x-1 (Theorem 4)
theorems.statement: For x>0: ln x ≤ x-1, with equality only at x=1 (the curve y=ln x lies below its tangent line y=x-1 at (1,0)).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given an initial value and one later data point, find k, then use it to predict the value at a third time.
question_archetypes.example: A bacteria culture has 500 cells initially and 800 after 24 h. How many after a further 12 h (t=36)?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two data points (an initial amount and one amount at a later, specific time) are given, and a third, different time is asked about — classic 'find k first' setup.
method_plan: Write y(t) = y0·e^(kt) using the given initial value as y0
Substitute the second data point to solve for k (usually left as k = (1/t1)·ln(ratio) rather than a decimal)
Substitute the target time into y(t) with this k
State the numeric answer in context, rounded sensibly
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct model y=y0 e^(kt) with y0 identified
M1: correct equation set up and solved for k
A1: correct substitution and evaluation at the target time
A1: answer stated in context with correct rounding

common_errors.description: Arithmetic slip solving for k or evaluating the final exponential
Rounding k too early, propagating error into the final answer (should keep k exact/symbolic until the last step)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given the growth/decay model and constant k (or the data to find it), solve for the time t at which the quantity reaches a specified target value.
question_archetypes.example: A radioactive substance decays with y(0)=100 and y(5)=80. How long until only 20 remain?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks 'how long until...' or 'when does the quantity reach...' — solve the exponential equation for t rather than for y.
method_plan: Set up y(t)=y0 e^(kt) and find k from the given data if not already known
Set y(t) equal to the target value
Divide by y0 and take ln of both sides
Solve for t and interpret in context
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct value of k obtained/used
M1: correct equation formed with the target value
A1: correct algebraic solve using ln
A1: sensible final numeric answer with units

common_errors.description: Confusing which exponent is growth (k>0) vs decay (k<0) and getting a nonsensical (negative time or wrong-direction) answer
Error isolating t after taking ln

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a growth/decay rate expressed as a percent per unit time, translate into k and use the model to answer a percent-remaining or percent-grown question.
question_archetypes.example: A population grows continuously at 3% per year. What percent increase occurs over 10 years?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The rate is stated as a percentage (e.g. '3% per year' or 'decays at 2% per hour') rather than as raw data points — directly gives k as the decimal rate, no data-fitting step needed.
method_plan: Convert the percent rate to k as a decimal (k = rate/100, with sign matching growth/decay)
Write y(t) = y0 e^(kt)
Evaluate at the given time and compare to y0 to get percent change
State as a percent increase or decrease
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct k identified directly from the stated rate
M1: correct evaluation of e^(kt) at the given time
A1: correctly converted to a percent change and interpreted

common_errors.description: Confusing a continuously-compounded percent rate with a simple/discrete percent rate (using (1+rate)^t instead of e^(kt))
Reporting the raw ratio (e.g. 1.3499) instead of converting it to '35% increase'

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a purely verbal description (no explicit equation), identify that the situation is modeled by dy/dt=ky and write down the correct model before solving.
question_archetypes.example: A rumor spreads through a population such that its rate of spread at any time is proportional to the number of people who already know it. Write a differential equation model and its general solution.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The phrase 'rate of change proportional to the amount present/remaining' appears in the problem statement — the direct verbal signature of dy/dt=ky, before any numbers are even given.
method_plan: Translate 'rate proportional to the quantity' into dy/dt = ky
State the general solution y = Ce^(kt)
If initial data is given, specialize to y=y0 e^(kt)
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct differential equation written from the verbal description
A1: correct general solution stated

common_errors.description: Misreading 'proportional to' and setting up a different (e.g. linear or logistic) model without justification
Jumping straight to a numeric answer without stating the governing differential equation when asked to model

micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute and use the constant doubling time or half-life of an exponential growth/decay process
definitions: Doubling time T (growth) or half-life T (decay) satisfies e^(kT)=2 or e^(kT)=1/2 respectively.
y(t+T) = 2y(t) (doubling) or (1/2)y(t) (halving) for ANY t — the doubling/halving time is constant, independent of the starting time.
formulas: T = ln(1/2)/k = -ln2/k  (half-life, k<0, T reported as positive)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given two data points of a decaying quantity, find k and then compute the half-life.
question_archetypes.example: A radioactive sample decays from 100g to 80g in 5 years. Find its half-life.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly asks for 'half-life' (or 'doubling time') rather than an amount at a given time — solve for T using e^(kT)=1/2, not for y(t).
method_plan: Find k from the given data (as in the basic growth/decay setup)
Set e^(kT) = 1/2 and take ln of both sides
Solve T = -ln2/k, reporting a positive value
State with correct units
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct k found from given data
M1: correct equation e^(kT)=1/2 set up and solved
A1: correct positive value with units

common_errors.description: Sign confusion producing a negative half-life (forgetting k<0 for decay)
Confusing the half-life formula with the doubling-time formula (using ln2 vs ln(1/2) inconsistently)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a growth rate k (or data to find it), compute the doubling time T=ln2/k.
question_archetypes.example: A population grows according to y'=0.04y. Find the doubling time.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: k is given directly (or easily extracted) and the question asks specifically for doubling time — a one-line application of T=ln2/k once k is known.
method_plan: Identify k directly from the given rate equation
Apply T = ln2/k
State the numeric value with units
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct k identified from y'=ky
A1: correct doubling time computed

common_errors.description: Confusing k with the doubling time itself, or with a percent rate not yet converted to k
Arithmetic slip computing ln2/k

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a known half-life, find the percent remaining after a specified (typically short) time, or the time to lose a given percent — using the constant-ratio property rather than re-deriving k from scratch data.
question_archetypes.example: A substance has half-life 1200 years. What percent remains after 10 years, and how long to lose 10%?
question_archetypes.answer: ≈99.42% remains after 10 years; ≈182.4 years to lose 10%.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The half-life is given as a stated fact (not derived from two data points), and the question asks about a time interval that is small relative to the half-life or about losing a specific fraction — use k=-ln2/T directly rather than fitting new data.
method_plan: Recover k from the given half-life via k = -ln2/T
Write p(t) = 100e^(kt) (as a percent model)
For 'percent remaining', substitute the given t
For 'time to lose X%', set p(t)=100-X and solve for t
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct k recovered from the half-life
M1: correct percent-remaining evaluation
M1: correct equation set up for the 'time to lose X%' part
A1: correct final answers for both parts

common_errors.description: Using T (the half-life) directly as if it were k
Sign or log-manipulation error solving for t in the second part

micro_skills.micro_skill: Set up and solve Newton's Law of Cooling problems by shifting to the ambient temperature
definitions: For a quantity relaxing toward an ambient value a: dy/dt = k(y-a).
Substituting u=y-a reduces this to u'=ku, so u=u0 e^(kt), i.e. y(t) = a + (y0-a)e^(kt).
The raw quantity y does NOT itself satisfy y'=ky — only the shifted quantity u=y-a does; forgetting this shift is the signature error in this topic.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: An object cools from one temperature to another over a known time in a room of known ambient temperature; find k, then predict the temperature at a further time.
question_archetypes.example: Coffee cools from 80°C to 50°C in 5 min in a 20°C room. How much longer to reach 40°C?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A temperature (or similar quantity like concentration) is said to approach a stated ambient/background value — the presence of an explicit 'room temperature' or 'surrounding medium' value is the cue to shift by that ambient value before treating it as pure exponential decay.
method_plan: Define u = y - a (temperature minus ambient)
Compute u0 = y0 - a and the value of u at the known later time
Solve for k using u(t1)=u0 e^(k t1)
Set u(t) equal to (target temp - a) and solve for t; subtract off any time already elapsed if the question asks for 'additional' time
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct shift u=y-a set up with correct u0
M1: correct k found from the given data point
M1: correct equation formed for the target temperature
A1: correct final time, with 'additional time' interpreted correctly if asked

common_errors.description: Applying y=y0 e^(kt) directly to the raw temperature without subtracting the ambient temperature first — the signature Newton's-cooling error
Reporting total elapsed time when the question asked for additional time beyond the given data point, or vice versa

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given k already known (or found from data), solve for the specific time at which the object reaches a new target temperature.
question_archetypes.example: An object at 100°C cools in a 25°C room with k=-0.05 (per minute). When does it reach 30°C?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question directly asks 'when/how long until temperature reaches ___' with k already given or easily found — solve for t via the shifted exponential equation.
method_plan: Shift to u=y-a and identify u0
Compute the target value of u = (target temperature - a)
Set u0 e^(kt) equal to the target u and take ln of both sides
Solve for t and check the sign/magnitude makes physical sense
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct target u value computed
M1: correct equation solved using ln
A1: correct final time with sensible sign

common_errors.description: Sign error in the exponent or in taking ln of a value between 0 and 1
Forgetting to subtract the ambient temperature when computing the 'target u' value

question_archetypes.prompt_template: An object colder than its surroundings warms up toward the ambient temperature (rather than cooling down) — same model, opposite direction, testing whether the student mechanically applies the formula rather than the underlying physics.
question_archetypes.example: A can of soda at 5°C is placed in a 25°C room and warms to 15°C in 20 minutes. Estimate its temperature after 1 hour.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The object's initial temperature is BELOW the ambient temperature (a warming, not cooling, scenario) — the same y=a+(y0-a)e^(kt) formula applies unchanged, but y0-a is now negative and k is still negative (approaching a from below).
method_plan: Identify a (ambient), y0 (initial, below a), and set up u=y-a (negative initially)
Use the given data point to solve for k
Substitute the target time into y(t)=a+(y0-a)e^(kt)
Sanity check the answer is between y0 and a and increasing toward a
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification that y0<a and correct sign handling
M1: correct k solved from the data
A1: correct final temperature, sanity-checked to lie between y0 and a

common_errors.description: Assuming warming requires a different formula or a positive k, rather than recognizing the same model with y0<a still gives k<0
Final answer not sanity-checked against the physically required range (y0, a)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Apply the continuous-compounding model to find growth time, future value, or compare compounding schemes
definitions: $A invested at nominal rate r% compounded continuously grows to $A·e^(r/100) in one year.
This follows from e^x = lim(n→∞) (1+x/n)^n (Theorem 6).
formulas: A(t) = A0·e^(rt)  (r as a decimal rate, t in years)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a principal, a continuous nominal rate, and a target amount, solve for the time required.
question_archetypes.example: How long for $1000 to grow to $2000 at nominal 6% compounded continuously?
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly says 'compounded continuously' with a stated nominal rate — directly use A=A0 e^(rt) with r as a decimal, no need to fit k from data.
method_plan: Write A(t)=A0 e^(rt) with r as a decimal (rate/100)
Set A(t) equal to the target amount
Divide by A0 and take ln
Solve for t
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct model with r correctly converted from percent to decimal
M1: correct equation solved using ln
A1: correct final time

common_errors.description: Forgetting to convert the percent rate to a decimal before using it as r
Confusing continuous compounding (e^(rt)) with periodic compounding ((1+r/n)^(nt))

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a principal, continuous rate, and time, compute the resulting amount directly.
question_archetypes.example: Find the value after 8 years of $5000 invested at a nominal 4.5% compounded continuously.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks directly for a future value ('how much will it be worth after...') with both rate and time given — a direct plug-in, no equation-solving for an unknown exponent needed.
method_plan: Convert the percent rate to a decimal
Substitute principal, rate, and time into A=A0 e^(rt)
Evaluate numerically
Round to appropriate currency precision
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution into the model
A1: correct numeric evaluation rounded appropriately

common_errors.description: Rate not converted from percent to decimal
Answer not rounded to a sensible currency precision (e.g. 2 decimal places)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compare continuous compounding to periodic (annual/monthly) compounding at the same nominal rate, using Theorem 6 as justification for why continuous compounding is the limiting case.
question_archetypes.example: Compare the value after 1 year of $1000 at 8% compounded (a) annually, (b) monthly, (c) continuously.
question_archetypes.answer: (a) $1080; (b) $1000(1+0.08/12)^12 ≈ $1083.00; (c) $1000e^0.08 ≈ $1083.29 — continuous is the largest, as the limiting case of increasingly frequent compounding.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly asks to 'compare' compounding frequencies or asks 'why is continuous compounding the limit of...' — a conceptual archetype tying back to Theorem 6.
method_plan: Compute the periodic-compounding value(s) using A0(1+r/n)^(nt)
Compute the continuous-compounding value using A0 e^(rt)
Compare the numeric results
Explain via Theorem 6 why continuous compounding is the n→∞ limit of periodic compounding
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct periodic compounding calculation(s)
A1: correct continuous compounding calculation
A1: correct numeric comparison stated
A1: correct conceptual link to Theorem 6

common_errors.description: Believing continuous compounding gives a dramatically larger result than frequent periodic compounding, rather than a marginally larger one (the limit converges)
Errors evaluating (1+r/n)^(nt) for large n

micro_skills.micro_skill: Set up and use the logistic growth model for population growth limited by a carrying capacity
definitions: dy/dt = ky(1 - y/L) models growth limited by a carrying capacity L.
Solution with y(0)=y0: y(t) = L·y0 / (y0 + (L-y0)e^(-kt)).
lim(t→∞) y(t) = L for 0<y0<L — the population approaches but never exceeds the carrying capacity.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a logistic differential equation or a verbal description ('growth rate proportional to both the population and the remaining room to capacity'), identify k, L, and y0 and write the explicit solution.
question_archetypes.example: A population satisfies dy/dt = 0.02y(1-y/5000) with y(0)=200. Write y(t) explicitly.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The differential equation has the explicit form ky(1-y/L) (or the problem states a 'carrying capacity') — distinguishes it from plain exponential growth dy/dt=ky.
method_plan: Identify k and L directly from the differential equation's coefficients
Identify y0 from the initial condition
Substitute all three into the logistic solution formula
Simplify the resulting expression
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct k and L identified
M1: correct y0 identified
A1: correctly substituted and simplified explicit formula

common_errors.description: Treating the logistic equation as plain exponential growth and using y=y0e^(kt) instead
Arithmetic slip computing L-y0

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a fully specified logistic model, evaluate the population at a specific future time.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A logistic formula (with the characteristic 1/(1+Ce^(-kt))-style denominator) is already given explicitly, and a specific numeric time is requested — a direct evaluation, not a setup problem.
method_plan: Substitute the given time into the logistic formula
Evaluate the exponential term
Simplify the fraction
Round appropriately
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution
A1: correct numeric evaluation

common_errors.description: Arithmetic slip evaluating the exponential or the resulting fraction

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine the long-run (t→∞) behavior of a logistic population and explain why it approaches the carrying capacity rather than growing without bound, contrasting with pure exponential growth.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why, for logistic growth with 0<y0<L, y(t)→L as t→∞, and contrast this with the unbounded growth of y=y0e^(kt).
question_archetypes.answer: As t→∞, e^(-kt)→0 (for k>0), so the denominator y0+(L-y0)e^(-kt) → y0, giving y(t)→L·y0/y0=L; pure exponential growth has no such limiting term and grows without bound.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks for a limit as t→∞ or explicitly asks to 'explain the long-run behavior' of a logistic model — a conceptual archetype about the structure of the formula rather than a numeric evaluation.
method_plan: Take the limit of the logistic formula as t→∞, noting e^(-kt)→0 for k>0
Simplify the resulting limit to L
Contrast with the unbounded exponential model, explaining the role of the (1-y/L) factor in the ODE
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct limit evaluated (denominator →y0)
A1: correct conclusion y(t)→L
A1: clear conceptual contrast with unbounded exponential growth

common_errors.description: Believing logistic growth eventually behaves like exponential growth forever, ignoring the carrying-capacity term
Stating the limit is L without showing the limiting argument on e^(-kt)

micro_skills.subtopic: Comparing Growth Rates of Exponentials, Powers, and Logs
micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate limits comparing the relative growth rates of exponential, power, and logarithmic functions

theorems.name: Theorem 5 (growth rates)
theorems.statement: For any a>0: lim(x→∞) x^a/e^x = 0; lim(x→∞) ln x/x^a = 0; lim(x→-∞) |x|^a e^x = 0; lim(x→0+) x^a ln x = 0.
conditions: appropriate one-sided or infinite limit as specified

formulas: Rule of thumb: exponentials beat powers, powers beat logs, as x→∞.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate lim(x→∞) of a power of x divided by e^x (or a similar exponential), directly quoting the growth-rate hierarchy.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate lim(x→∞) x^5/e^x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The limit is a polynomial or power of x divided by (or multiplied by, at -∞) an exponential as x→∞ — instant recognition case for Theorem 5, faster than repeated l'Hôpital.
method_plan: Recognize the form x^a/e^x as x→∞
Cite Theorem 5 (exponentials dominate powers) directly
State the limit is 0
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct limit value with Theorem 5 cited as justification (or repeated l'Hôpital shown to the same conclusion)

common_errors.description: Grinding through five rounds of l'Hôpital's Rule instead of directly citing the known growth-rate result
Believing a high power of x eventually overtakes an exponential

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate lim(x→∞) of ln x divided by a power of x, or lim(x→0+) of a power times ln x.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate lim(x→∞) (ln x)/sqrt(x) and lim(x→0+) x^2 ln x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: One factor is ln x and the other is a power of x, evaluated either as x→∞ (power in denominator) or x→0+ (power multiplying ln x, an ∞·0 form) — both are direct instances of Theorem 5.
method_plan: For the x→∞ case, recognize ln x/x^a→0 directly from Theorem 5
For the x→0+ case, recognize x^a ln x→0 directly from Theorem 5 (an indeterminate 0·(-∞) form resolved by the theorem)
State both limits with justification
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct first limit with justification
A1: correct second limit with justification

common_errors.description: Treating x^2 ln x at x→0+ as automatically 0 without recognizing it is an indeterminate 0·(-∞) form needing this specific result
Using l'Hôpital on the x→0+ case without first rewriting it as a quotient

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate lim(x→-∞) of |x|^a·e^x, recognizing that e^x→0 dominates any polynomial growth in |x|^a.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate lim(x→-∞) x^4 e^x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The limit is as x→-∞ specifically, with a power of x multiplying e^x (not divided) — a variant of the growth-rate hierarchy that students often mishandle by expecting the answer to blow up.
method_plan: Recognize the form |x|^a e^x as x→-∞ from Theorem 5
Note that as x→-∞, e^x→0 much faster than any polynomial in x grows
State the limit is 0
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct limit stated with correct justification (Theorem 5, x→-∞ case)

common_errors.description: Assuming the limit diverges because x^4→∞, without accounting for e^x→0 dominating
Attempting substitution u=-x and mishandling the resulting sign/form

micro_skills.subtopic: Inverse Trig Functions: Domains, Ranges, Exact Values
micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate inverse trig functions at exact values, respecting the restricted range of each
definitions: sin^-1 x (arcsin): restriction of sin to [-π/2,π/2]; domain [-1,1]; range [-π/2,π/2].
cos^-1 x (arccos): restriction of cos to [0,π]; domain [-1,1]; range [0,π].
tan^-1 x (arctan): restriction of tan to (-π/2,π/2); domain ℝ; range (-π/2,π/2).
sec^-1 x: restriction of sec to [0,π/2)∪(π/2,π]; domain |x|≥1; range [0,π/2)∪(π/2,π].
csc^-1 x = sin^-1(1/x); cot^-1 x = tan^-1(1/x).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an inverse trig function at a standard value (e.g. ±1, ±1/2, ±1/√2, ±√3/2), giving the answer in the correct restricted range.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate sin^-1(-1/sqrt2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The input is one of the standard trig values (1, 1/2, √2/2, √3/2, etc.) — recall the reference angle, then adjust its sign/quadrant to land inside the specific inverse function's range.
method_plan: Recall the reference angle whose sine/cosine/tangent equals the given value in magnitude
Determine the correct sign/quadrant using the specific range of the inverse function involved
State the angle within that range (typically in radians)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct reference angle identified
A1: correct sign/quadrant chosen to match the function's range
A1: answer given in the expected units (radians unless told otherwise)

common_errors.description: Using the wrong function's range (e.g. picking a cos^-1-range angle for an arcsin problem)
Sign error when the input is negative

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate sec^-1 (or csc^-1, cot^-1) using the reciprocal-relation definitions, being careful with the less-standard restricted range.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate sec^-1(-2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The inverse function involved is sec^-1, csc^-1, or cot^-1 rather than the three primary inverses — these have less-memorized, easy-to-misremember restricted ranges.
method_plan: Rewrite in terms of the primary inverse function if needed (e.g. csc^-1x = sin^-1(1/x))
Recall the specific restricted range for the function involved
Find the angle within that range whose corresponding trig ratio matches
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct rewriting into a primary inverse trig function if applicable
A1: correct angle found within the correct restricted range

common_errors.description: Using the arcsin/arccos range instead of the correct sec^-1/csc^-1/cot^-1 range
Sign error converting between the function and its reciprocal

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an inverse trig function composed with itself outside the 'obvious' range (e.g. sin^-1(sin(3π/4))), requiring the supplementary/reference-angle correction rather than naive cancellation.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate sin^-1(sin(3π/4)).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The inner angle given to sin^-1(sin(·)) (or the analogous cos^-1(cos(·)), tan^-1(tan(·))) visibly lies outside that inverse function's range — the identity f^-1(f(θ))=θ only cancels directly when θ is already inside the range.
method_plan: Check whether the inner angle already lies in the inverse function's range
If not, find an angle in the correct range with the same trig value (using symmetry/supplementary-angle identities)
State that equivalent angle as the final answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly identifies the inner angle is outside the valid range
M1: correctly finds an equivalent angle within the range using a trig identity
A1: correct final numeric answer

common_errors.description: Naively canceling sin^-1(sin(θ))=θ without checking θ lies in [-π/2,π/2] first
Using the wrong supplementary/reference-angle relationship for the specific function involved

micro_skills.subtopic: Composing Trig Functions with Inverse Trig Functions
micro_skills.micro_skill: Simplify expressions like cos(tan^-1 x) or tan(sin^-1 x) using a reference right triangle
definitions: To simplify trig(inverse-trig(x)), let θ = inverse-trig(x), draw a right triangle matching the definition of θ, label the two given sides, find the third via the Pythagorean theorem, then read off the requested ratio.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a composition like cos(tan^-1 2) where the inner inverse trig function has a specific numeric input, using a reference triangle.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate cos(tan^-1 2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A trig function is applied to an inverse trig function of a specific number (not a variable x) — build a right triangle with the given ratio as two of its sides, then read off the requested trig ratio.
method_plan: Let θ = the inner inverse trig expression
Draw a right triangle with sides matching the definition of θ (e.g. opposite=2, adjacent=1 for tan θ=2)
Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side
Read off the requested outer trig ratio from the triangle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct triangle set up with two correct side labels
M1: correct third side via Pythagorean theorem
A1: correct final ratio read from the triangle

common_errors.description: Mislabeling which sides are opposite/adjacent for the given inverse trig function
Not checking whether θ could be in a different quadrant, missing a sign (relevant when the input is negative)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Simplify a composition like tan(sin^-1 x) for a general variable x (not a specific number), producing an algebraic expression in x.
question_archetypes.example: Simplify tan(sin^-1 x) for |x|<1.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The inner inverse trig function has a variable x as its argument (not a number) — the reference triangle has sides labeled with x and 1, and the answer is an algebraic function of x, valid on a stated domain.
method_plan: Let θ = sin^-1 x (or the relevant inverse function), so the defining ratio equals x/1
Draw the triangle with opposite=x, hypotenuse=1 (or as appropriate for the given inverse function)
Find the missing side using Pythagoras, in terms of x
Read off the requested outer trig ratio as an expression in x, stating the valid domain
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct triangle labeled with x as a side/ratio
M1: correct missing side found in terms of x
A1: correct final expression with domain noted if relevant

common_errors.description: Omitting the domain restriction (e.g. |x|<1) under which the simplification is valid
Sign error under the square root when finding the missing side

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Prove an identity involving inverse trig functions (e.g. tan^-1((x-1)/(x+1)) = tan^-1 x - π/4) by differentiating both sides and matching a constant via a convenient test value.
question_archetypes.example: Prove tan^-1((x-1)/(x+1)) = tan^-1 x - π/4 for x>-1.
question_archetypes.answer: Both sides have equal derivative 1/(1+x^2), so their difference is constant; evaluating at x=0 confirms the constant is 0, proving the identity.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem says 'prove' or 'show' an equation between two inverse-trig expressions holds for all x in some domain — the standard technique is to show the derivative of (LHS-RHS) is zero, then pin down the constant with one convenient value.
method_plan: Differentiate both sides of the claimed identity using the chain rule for tan^-1(g(x))
Show the two derivatives are equal, so LHS-RHS is constant on the domain
Evaluate both sides at one convenient x-value to determine the constant
Conclude the constant is 0 (or whatever value matches), proving the identity
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivative of the LHS
M1: correct derivative of the RHS
A1: correctly concludes the derivatives match, so the difference is constant
A1: correctly evaluates at a test point to pin down the constant and complete the proof

common_errors.description: Forgetting the chain-rule factor when differentiating tan^-1 of a quotient
Omitting the final test-value step, leaving the constant undetermined and the proof incomplete

micro_skills.micro_skill: Differentiate expressions involving the inverse trig functions, with and without the chain rule

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate sin^-1(g(x)) or cos^-1(g(x)) for a non-trivial inner function g(x) using the chain rule.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = sin^-1(3x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: sin^-1 or cos^-1 wraps a linear or otherwise non-x inner function — multiply the base formula by the inner derivative and adjust the expression under the square root accordingly.
method_plan: Identify the inner function g(x)
Apply d/dx sin^-1(g) = g'(x)/sqrt(1-g(x)^2)
Simplify the expression under the square root
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct base formula recalled
M1: correct chain-rule inner derivative
A1: correctly simplified final answer

common_errors.description: Forgetting to square the inner function under the square root (writing sqrt(1-3x) instead of sqrt(1-9x^2))
Forgetting the chain-rule multiplier g'(x) entirely

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate tan^-1(g(x)) for a non-trivial inner function using the chain rule, then use the result to identify a corresponding integral.
question_archetypes.example: Find d/dx tan^-1(3x) and use it to evaluate ∫ dx/(1+9x^2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: tan^-1 wraps a linear inner function and the problem explicitly links the derivative to a corresponding indefinite integral — a two-part 'differentiate then integrate the reverse' archetype.
method_plan: Differentiate tan^-1(g(x)) using g'(x)/(1+g(x)^2)
Simplify
Recognize the target integral as (1/inner-derivative-constant) times the derivative just found
State the antiderivative with +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivative of tan^-1(3x)
M1: correctly relates the derivative to the target integral form
A1: correct antiderivative with the 1/3 scaling and +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting to rescale by 1/3 when going from the derivative back to the integral
Omitting +C in the final integral answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate sec^-1(g(x)), carefully including the absolute value in the formula.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = sec^-1(2x) for x>1/2.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is sec^-1 (or csc^-1) — the only inverse-trig derivative with an absolute value in its formula, easy to drop by analogy with the other three.
method_plan: Recall the formula d/dx sec^-1(g) = g'(x)/(|g(x)|sqrt(g(x)^2-1))
Apply the chain rule with the specific inner function
Simplify, using the given domain restriction to resolve the absolute value if possible
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct formula recalled including |g(x)|
M1: correct chain-rule inner derivative
A1: correctly simplified, with the absolute value resolved using the stated domain if applicable

common_errors.description: Dropping the absolute value bars entirely (writing g(x) instead of |g(x)| in the denominator)
Not resolving |2x| using the given domain, leaving an unnecessarily complicated final answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate an expression combining an inverse trig function with another factor via the product or quotient rule.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = x·tan^-1(x) - (1/2)ln(1+x^2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: An inverse trig function appears multiplied by (or combined with) another x-dependent factor, and the terms are constructed so that some cancellation occurs — signals both product rule and simplification are needed, and a clean answer is a strong hint the algebra was done correctly.
method_plan: Apply the product rule to the term(s) containing the inverse trig factor
Differentiate any accompanying ln or other term with the chain rule
Combine and simplify all terms, watching for cancellation
State the simplified final derivative
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct product rule applied to the inverse-trig term
M1: correct derivative of the remaining term(s)
A1: correctly simplified/cancelled final answer

common_errors.description: Forgetting the product rule and only differentiating the inverse trig factor
Missing the cancellation that was meant to simplify the answer, submitting an unsimplified expression

micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate integrals whose antiderivatives are sin^-1 or tan^-1 expressions, including after algebraic preparation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral of the form ∫dx/sqrt(a^2-x^2) directly, or after rescaling to identify a and matching the pattern.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate ∫ dx/sqrt(9-x^2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand has a square root of (constant minus x^2) in the denominator with no other x-dependence — direct match to the arcsin antiderivative pattern with a^2 equal to that constant.
method_plan: Identify a^2 as the constant under the square root, so a=sqrt(constant)
Apply the formula ∫dx/sqrt(a^2-x^2) = sin^-1(x/a)+C directly
State the answer with +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of a
A1: correct final antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Using a instead of a^2 or vice versa when identifying the constant
Omitting +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral of the form ∫dx/(a^2+x^2), correctly including the 1/a scaling factor outside the tan^-1.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate ∫ dx/(4+x^2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is a constant over (constant + x^2), matching the tan^-1 antiderivative pattern — the easy-to-forget part is the 1/a multiplier out front, distinct from the arcsin case which has no such factor.
method_plan: Identify a^2 as the constant added to x^2, so a=sqrt(constant)
Apply ∫dx/(a^2+x^2) = (1/a)tan^-1(x/a)+C
State the answer with +C, double-checking the 1/a factor is included
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of a
A1: correct final antiderivative including the 1/a factor and +C

common_errors.description: Forgetting the 1/a scaling factor outside the tan^-1 (a common confusion with the arcsin formula, which has no such factor)
Omitting +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an integral that requires completing the square, factoring out a constant, or another algebraic manipulation before it matches the sin^-1 or tan^-1 pattern.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate ∫ dx/sqrt(8-2x^2) and ∫ dx/(x^2+4x+13).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The denominator does not immediately look like a^2±x^2 — a constant needs factoring out from under a root, or the quadratic needs completing the square, before the standard inverse-trig integral formula can be applied.
method_plan: For a square-root denominator, factor out the leading numeric coefficient of x^2 from inside the root
For a quadratic denominator, complete the square to write it as (x-h)^2 + k^2 or k^2-(x-h)^2
Substitute u=(x-h) so the integral matches the standard sin^-1 or tan^-1 pattern in u
Apply the formula and convert back to x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct algebraic preparation (factoring or completing the square)
M1: correct recognition of a and the substitution u=x-h
A1: correct antiderivative in terms of u
A1: correctly converted back to x with +C

common_errors.description: Error completing the square or factoring out the leading coefficient
Forgetting to substitute back from u to x, or dropping the shift (x-h) inside the inverse trig argument

micro_skills.micro_skill: Use the exponential definitions, fundamental identity, and derivative rules of the hyperbolic functions
definitions: cosh x = (e^x+e^-x)/2, sinh x = (e^x-e^-x)/2.
Fundamental identity: cosh^2 t - sinh^2 t = 1. cosh is even, sinh is odd; cosh0=1, sinh0=0.
tanh x = sinh x/cosh x, coth x = 1/tanh x, sech x = 1/cosh x, csch x = 1/sinh x.
tanh x → ±1 as x → ±∞ (two horizontal asymptotes).
formulas: d/dx cosh x = sinh x, d/dx sinh x = cosh x (no minus sign, unlike circular functions)
d/dx tanh x = sech^2 x, d/dx coth x = -csch^2 x, d/dx sech x = -sech x·tanh x, d/dx csch x = -csch x·coth x
cosh(x+y) = cosh x cosh y + sinh x sinh y, sinh(x+y) = sinh x cosh y + cosh x sinh y
cosh(2x) = cosh^2x + sinh^2x = 2cosh^2x-1, sinh(2x) = 2 sinh x cosh x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Verify a stated hyperbolic identity (e.g. the fundamental identity or a derivative formula) directly from the exponential definitions.
question_archetypes.example: Show cosh^2 x - sinh^2 x = 1 using the exponential definitions.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question says 'verify' or 'show' a hyperbolic identity — expand both cosh and sinh via their exponential definitions and simplify algebraically, rather than treating it as a memorized fact.
method_plan: Write cosh x and sinh x using their e^x, e^-x definitions
Square each and expand
Subtract (or combine as required by the identity) and simplify
Confirm the result matches the claimed identity
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct exponential expansion of both terms
A1: correct algebraic simplification to the claimed result

common_errors.description: Sign error expanding (e^x-e^-x)^2, particularly the cross term
Not showing the full expansion, jumping straight to '=1' without justification

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate a basic hyperbolic function or simple sum, being careful there is no sign flip (unlike sin/cos).
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = 3cosh x - 5sinh x + tanh x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A sum of hyperbolic functions is given directly (no composite/chain-rule structure) — the main risk is misapplying the trig sign convention out of habit.
method_plan: Differentiate each term using the hyperbolic derivative rules
Double check no minus sign is introduced for cosh'=sinh or sinh'=cosh
Combine with correct signs from the original coefficients
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct derivative of each term
A1: correct overall sign combination

common_errors.description: Using the trigonometric sign convention (writing d/dx cosh x = -sinh x) — the single most common hyperbolic-derivative mistake
Sign error combining the coefficients of the original sum

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate a composite hyperbolic function, e.g. sinh(g(x)) or tanh(g(x)), using the chain rule.
question_archetypes.example: Differentiate y = tanh(x^2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A hyperbolic function wraps a non-trivial inner function — apply the chain rule exactly as with circular trig functions (the derivative rule itself has no minus-sign trap here, only in the basic sinh/cosh case).
method_plan: Identify the inner function and its derivative
Apply the appropriate hyperbolic derivative formula to the outer function
Multiply by the inner derivative
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct outer hyperbolic derivative formula used
M1: correct inner derivative found
A1: correctly combined final answer

common_errors.description: Forgetting the chain-rule inner-derivative factor
Using the wrong hyperbolic derivative formula, e.g. confusing sech^2 with csch^2 for tanh vs coth

micro_skills.micro_skill: Derive and use the logarithmic forms of the inverse hyperbolic functions
definitions: Since cosh is not one-to-one on all of ℝ, its inverse requires restricting to x≥0 (principal value Cosh x).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive the ln formula for an inverse hyperbolic function from scratch by solving a quadratic in e^y.
question_archetypes.example: Express sinh^-1 x in terms of ln by solving the defining equation for y.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question says 'derive' or 'express in terms of ln, starting from the definition' — signals the quadratic-in-e^y technique rather than quoting the memorized formula.
method_plan: Let y = sinh^-1 x, so x = (e^y-e^-y)/2
Multiply both sides by 2e^y to clear the negative exponent, obtaining a quadratic in e^y
Solve the quadratic using the quadratic formula, keeping only the root with e^y>0
Take ln of both sides to solve for y
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct multiplication by 2e^y producing a quadratic in e^y
M1: correct application of the quadratic formula
A1: correct rejection of the extraneous (negative) root
A1: correct final ln expression

common_errors.description: Keeping both roots of the quadratic instead of rejecting the one that makes e^y negative or undefined
Sign/arithmetic error setting up or solving the quadratic

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a specific inverse hyperbolic expression numerically or symbolically using the ln formula directly.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate cosh^-1(2) exactly.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A specific numeric value is plugged into an inverse hyperbolic function — direct substitution into the memorized ln formula, no derivation required.
method_plan: Identify which inverse hyperbolic function is involved and recall its ln formula
Substitute the given value directly
Simplify under the square root if possible
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct formula recalled
A1: correct substitution and simplification

common_errors.description: Using the wrong inverse hyperbolic formula (mixing up sinh^-1, cosh^-1, tanh^-1)
Arithmetic error simplifying the value under the square root

question_archetypes.prompt_template: State and apply the correct domain restriction (x≥1 for cosh^-1, -1<x<1 for tanh^-1) when evaluating or working with an inverse hyperbolic expression, and explain why the restriction is necessary.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why cosh^-1 requires x≥1, and evaluate tanh^-1(0.5).
question_archetypes.answer: cosh is not one-to-one on all of ℝ (it's even), so its inverse must restrict to x≥0 to be well-defined; tanh^-1(0.5) = (1/2)ln(1.5/0.5) = (1/2)ln3.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly asks about the domain restriction ('why must x≥1', 'for what x is this defined') or gives a value near the edge of a restricted domain — a conceptual check rather than pure computation.
method_plan: Recall which original hyperbolic function is not one-to-one on all of ℝ (cosh, being even) and why restricting to x≥0 is needed
State the resulting domain of each inverse hyperbolic function
Evaluate the requested expression using the ln formula, confirming the input lies in the valid domain
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct explanation of the domain restriction and its cause
M1: correct formula applied for the evaluation
A1: correct final numeric/symbolic value

common_errors.description: Not recognizing that cosh^-1's domain restriction stems from cosh failing to be one-to-one (evenness), rather than an arbitrary convention
Evaluating tanh^-1 at a value outside (-1,1) without flagging that it is undefined there

micro_skills.subtopic: Simplifying and Proving Results with Hyperbolic Functions
micro_skills.micro_skill: Simplify composite hyperbolic expressions and use hyperbolic functions to solve/verify second-order ODEs

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Simplify a hyperbolic function evaluated at a logarithmic (or otherwise composite) argument, converting back to an algebraic expression in x.
question_archetypes.example: Simplify tanh(ln x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A hyperbolic function is applied to ln x (or another expression that will make e^(that expression) simplify nicely) — expand via the exponential definitions and the e^(ln x)=x cancellation.
method_plan: Write the hyperbolic function using its exponential definition
Substitute the given argument and use e^(ln x)=x, e^(-ln x)=1/x to simplify each exponential term
Combine into a single algebraic fraction in x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct exponential-definition expansion
M1: correct use of the ln/exp cancellation identities
A1: correctly simplified final algebraic expression

common_errors.description: Sign or fraction-combination error simplifying (x-1/x)/(x+1/x)-type expressions
Forgetting e^(-ln x)=1/x and instead treating it as -x or another incorrect form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Show that a linear combination of e^(kt) and e^(-kt) solves y''-k^2y=0, and re-express the solution using cosh and sinh.
question_archetypes.example: Show that f(t)=Ae^(kt)+Be^(-kt) solves y''-k^2y=0, and express it using cosh, sinh.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives a combination of e^(kt) and e^(-kt) and asks either to verify a second-order ODE or to rewrite it in terms of cosh/sinh — the exponential combination is a strong visual cue for a hyperbolic rewrite.
method_plan: Differentiate the given f(t) twice
Substitute into y''-k^2y and confirm it equals 0
Group the e^(kt) and e^(-kt) terms to match the definitions of cosh(kt) and sinh(kt)
State the equivalent cosh/sinh form with the correct combined coefficients
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct second derivative computed
A1: correct verification that f''-k^2f=0
M1: correct grouping into cosh(kt), sinh(kt) form
A1: correct final coefficients (A+B) and (A-B)

common_errors.description: Error identifying which coefficient combination (A+B) vs (A-B) goes with cosh vs sinh
Not simplifying k^2 f(t) back in terms of the original f, leaving the ODE verification incomplete
